newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU finance ministers near EMU pact deal.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers near EMU pact deal.

text.p: European Union finance ministers made good progress on Sunday towards finalising a stability pact and resolving a row between France and Germany, the two main powers behind the push to monetary union.
Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told a news conference after ministers from the 15 member states attended an informal dinner that a text on a pact could be finalised on Monday.
"We made extremely good progress...we will be able to finish a text (on the stability pact) tomorrow (Monday)," he said.
Italian Finance Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said the meeting had been positive and that the positions of the 15 members were close, raising expectations of a deal.
Belgium's Philippe Maystadt said the ministers would continue their negotiations at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Monday.
Germany and France, the primary engines behind Europe's drive for monetary union, have been at odds over how to proceed towards a single currency, due to be launched in January 1999.
The stability pact was agreed in principle at a Dublin summit last December after tough negotiations and was due to be approved by EU leaders in Amsterdam this week.

But last week France's new socialist government stunned EU partners by demanding more time to study the stability pact, a framework for keeping EU budgets from ballooning into deficit after the planned euro currency is introduced.

French premier Lionel Jospin insists he wants a bigger profile given to creating jobs for some of the bloc's 18 million unemployed and opposes the economic austerity required to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Germany is against any weakening of the single currency criteria and any job creation schemes which involve pumping huge sums of public cash into grand finance projects.

Austrian Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger told reporters that the finance ministers had agreed not to reveal publicly any details of Sunday's discussions, other than to say that a likely deal would hinge on two issues.
"The decisions will be on the growth and stability pact on one hand and employment on the other," he said.
Edlinger said that EU leaders would decide on Monday whether or not to hold a special summit in October to discuss the bloc's high unemployment.
A "jobs summit" was seen by officials as one possible way to acknowledge French demands without making immediate promises to commit funds to job creation programmes.
Sweden's Erik Asbrink said the finance ministers had discussed the possibility of giving the European Investment Bank (EIB) a more active role.
"Can we extend the scope of the bank's activities?... That is something we are looking at," he told reporters after the eve-of-summit dinner.
Asbrink said it was possible the EIB would form part of a resolution on employment which was very likely to be agreed during the summit which begins on Monday.

He said the meeting had not discussed the issue of a stability council to give a political counterbalance to the future European Central Bank -- another French demand, adding that this would be discussed during the Luxembourg EU presidency during the second half of 1997.
He said there had not been detailed discussion about funding for trans-European rail and road networks, an area where France had suggested extra spending as a way to boost jobs in Europe.
